Among the recovered materials from the cart, you will have secured an <color=green>Anvil</color>.

With it, you may construct a Primitive Ironworks — and with ironworks, we may finally speak of real engineering.

To supply it, establish a Scavenger Flag and begin collecting Scrap Metal from nearby ruins.

In addition, construct a Primitive Mine. It may extract Iron Ore or Coal, both of which can be refined into scrap metal within an <color=green>Ore Smelter</color>. Alternatively, coal can be obtained from the <color=green>woodburner</color>, should your tendency to destroy the environment have already got the best of you.

With this, you can at last build a proper dam and make droughts easier on your people.

Accidentally, you might even make your mother proud. And surpised.

Only psychopaths would snack on Kimchi all day. Sane beavers will also require <color=green>Sunflower Seeds</color> and <color=green>Berries</color> to munch on.

Plant Sunflowers if you have not done so already.

Construct appropriate storage for the seeds. As with Rice — and all other granular materials — they are to be kept in a Pile.

We are aware that certain heretics prefer to box them up. Our seeds have not committed any crime yet.

Your Foresters are probably still unable to plant new berry bushes. This is a recurring issue in new settlements.

<color=green>Protect the ones you have as much as possible</color>.

Hello.

I am currently answering messages on behalf of the Directorate of Applied Chemistry and Public Health.

The previous staff appear to have… vacated their positions. Quite suddenly. I really hope they didn't get into trouble again.

The authorities have asked that we immediately report any sightings of funny-smelling chemists who should not be left unsupervised around… well, anything really. Possibly pencils and paper.

Speaking of which, I have found a note instructing me to continue the chemical program. It says: “Next step: Brain-Boosting Salts.”

If I remember my classes correctly, this requires the production of <color=green>Alcohol</color>.

To obtain alcohol, you will first need fermentable ingredients. You may proceed in either of the following ways:

- Plant <color=green>Rice</color> in <color=#00FFFF>shallow water</color> in the river.
- Plant <color=green>Chestnut Trees</color> wherever they might look nice.

Then please construct two additional stacks of Fermentation Barrels and configure them to produce either <color=green>Half-Fermented Sake</color> or <color=green>Chestnut Beer</color>, whichever is appropriate.

Your settlers will probably attempt to drink those, but worry not — the following headaches will quickly teach them moderation.

Off: no weather rolls at all. The mod stays loaded but the scheduler is silent.

Strict cycle lock: the vanilla cycle decides. Drought always rolls a sandstorm, badtide always rolls acid rain, temperate always rolls clean rain. However, if the cycle's expected weather is disabled (e.g. drought with sandstorms turned off), nothing rolls that event.

Biased (default): 90% chance the event matches the cycle, 5% each chance for the other two weather types. Lets the cycle do its thing most of the time while still giving you the occasional surprise. Disabled weather types redistribute their share to the others.

Random: the cycle is ignored entirely. Sandstorm chance and acid escalation sliders drive every roll.

Ah. You are still alive. Good.

It seems you have successfully produced <color=red>Brain Boosting Salts</color>, and since we — thankfully — did not hear back from the IPP bureau, we will assume you managed to duplicate your blueprints.

You may now construct a Floodgate Dam.

The objective of such a structure is not to stop water entirely — that is the thinking of amateurs and architects — but to redirect its flow according to your needs.

Properly placed floodgates allow you to guide water away from your reservoir during a Badtide, or toward your infrastructure when conditions are favorable.

Construct at least one Floodgate Dam and demonstrate to all that machines are superior to the forces of nature.

The guards take their posts near the old storage floor. They have water, berries, and the kind of courage that gets quieter the longer the night lasts. The Campfire burns behind them. The storage piles creak ahead of them. Beneath the raised plank, something shifts. Then the knocking comes. Knock. Knock. Knock. One guard calls out. Another steps closer. The floor erupts. A shadow bolts from below, fast and wild with panic. The guards close ranks, but the thing fights like it has already decided capture means death. By the time the colony reaches them, several guards are injured. A cup rolls across the dirt. Berries scatter underfoot. But the shadow has been caught. In the firelight, held down at last, lies an unconscious beaver no one recognizes. [[C]][[-]]{0} Beavers injured.

{0}
For two days, the captured beaver does not wake.
The injured are bandaged. The old storage floor is watched. The Campfire burns quietly, but no one asks for stories.
Then, at last, the stranger opens their eyes.
They are thin, frightened, and smaller than the shadow made them seem.
When they see the gathered colony, they scramble backward until their tail strikes the wall. It is crooked, scarred, and stiff, curled strangely enough that several beavers understand the spiral marks all at once.
The marks were not curses.
They were not warnings from a ghost.
They were tail-signs, scratched by someone who needed to find their way through the dark.
Piece by piece, the truth comes out.
The stranger came from a failed settlement beyond the trees. They followed the smoke of the Campfire, found the colony, and hid beneath the storage floor because hunger was easier to face than being chased away.
They stole only what they could carry.
They knocked because they were afraid.
They fought because, in the dark, every paw reaching down looked like an enemy.
{1}
Now the colony must decide what kind of story this will become.
A warning.
A welcome.
Or the tale of a beaver who found firelight and was sent back into the dark.

A studying session would only yield boredom if not supplemented with snacks, and by snacks we mean <color=green>Kimchi</color>.

To produce Kimchi, you will need <color=green>Bramble Flowers</color>, they are harvested by Lumberjacks. However, the task is… extensive. Assigning unqualified flag workers to the task would condemn them to a tedious and prickly existence.

Construct a Woodfelling Planification Lodge or a Lumberjack’s Barn near brambles so that properly qualified workers can take care of it. Qualified workers get a little hat, that is how you know they are qualified.

Also, <color=red>mark the brambles for cutting</color>. They will not volunteer.

Those buildings will require <color=green>Tools</color>. These are fabricated in the <color=green>Primitive Ironworks</color>. Competence works better with equipment.

While this is getting done, construct three stacks of Fermentation Barrels. Patience will convert sharpness into nourishment.

It seems you have managed to secure the basic necessities. Survival, however, is not the same as refinement.

With <color=green>Mushrooms</color> and <color=green>Cabbages</color>, you may now prepare <color=green>Braised Cabbage</color> — a meal properly cooked rather than merely harvested. You will find that cooking produces more nourishment than the simple sum of its ingredients.

This is not magic. It is organization.

To begin, construct a Clay Pit and extract Clay. Civilized meals require proper vessels, and proper vessels require proper materials.

Clay is stored in boxes, should you be interested in such trivia.

We Whitepaws do not merely survive. We dine.

Having consulted the instructional billboard, you may now construct the Rudimentary Sawmill.

In most circumstances, one or two Crappy Waterwheels will suffice to power it. Position them in flowing water. We trust you can identify flowing water without assistance.

Should you be fortunate enough to settle near a <color=green>Geothermal Field</color>, a <color=green>Geothermal Engine</color> is also acceptable.

However you choose to power it, ensure the sawmill is supplied with <color=green>sawblades</color>, those are made by the workers of your <color=green>primitive ironworks</color> who surely regret following you by now.

Should you decide to build a stock of those, sawblades are stored in piles.

To the Expedition Leader,

Your reports have been received.

It appears that your settlement is still alive and well, with a growing population.

More importantly, you have somehow endured contact with the administration without any threats, sabotage, or assassination attempts on either side. At least as far as we know.

We therefore conclude that further assistance is no longer necessary.

You and your settlement remain part of the proud Whitepaws nation. Do not allow our reduced supervision to affect your judgment.

Expand. Build. Study. Experiment.
Try not to destroy anything irreplaceable.

We wish you the best of luck.

You are still not welcome to come back. Success does not mean people have forgotten.

Greetings.

We represent the Directorate of Architectural Ambition, the body responsible for ensuring that settlements rise above crude piles of timber and become structures of elegance.

Your settlement, while… functional… currently demonstrates a worrying absence of architectural vision. Like most diseases, this is correctable.

Build an Architect’s Lodge so that your settlement may take its first step toward dignity.

This building will allow a trained Architect to assemble sturdy yet lightweight <color=green>Scaffoldings</color>, which form the foundation for walkways, platforms, upgrades, and other structural elements that allow settlements to grow vertically, rather than spreading like an undisciplined fungus across the landscape.

Postscript: You may notice that the <color=#FF6EC7>rear façade</color> of the building forms a large angled structure. This is not a <color=#FF6EC7>staircase</color>.

It is an architectural gesture intended to evoke upward motion and structural dynamism. Please do not allow your settlers to walk on it.

Yes, it is possible.

That does not make it acceptable.
